title: 《Nanomaterials at the Limit: Engineering Interfaces, Defects, Surfaces, and Programmable Matter》 is a flagship-scale research volume exploring what becomes possible when the properties of matter are no longer determined primarily by bulk composition, but by size, shape, surface, interface, defect structure, hierarchy, and nanoscale organization.
abstract: 《Nanomaterials at the Limit: Engineering Interfaces, Defects, Surfaces, and Programmable Matter》 is a flagship-scale research volume exploring what becomes possible when the properties of matter are no longer determined primarily by bulk composition, but by size, shape, surface, interface, defect structure, hierarchy, and nanoscale organization. The central question is: What kinds of materials can civilization design when structure itself becomes a controllable variable? At the nanoscale, matter behaves differently. Surface-to-volume ratio increases dramatically. Interfaces can dominate transport. Defects can become functional rather than merely undesirable. Quantum confinement can reshape electronic and optical behavior. Grain boundaries, pores, ligands, coatings, strain, topology, and local chemistry can alter macroscopic performance. This means that materials engineering begins to move beyond the traditional question: What is this material made of? and toward a deeper question: How is this material organized across multiple scales? The book develops this idea through the general framework: P_macro = F(d, shape, surface, interface, defect, composition, hierarchy) where macroscopic properties emerge from the coupled influence of nanoscale dimensions, morphology, interfaces, defects, chemistry, and hierarchical structure. This framework turns nanomaterials research into a broader design language. The objective is not simply to discover exotic nanoscale effects. It is to understand how those effects can be measured, stabilized, manufactured, reproduced, integrated, and eventually used in real systems. The book therefore introduces the Nano Functional Index: NFI = (Functional Gain_n × Stability_n × Scalability_n) / (1 + Defect Burden_n + Interface Loss_n + Criticality_n) The purpose of the NFI is not to declare one material universally superior. It is to force performance, durability, manufacturability, interface quality, defect sensitivity, and resource constraints into the same analytical frame. A nanomaterial with exceptional laboratory performance may still fail as an engineering platform if it is unstable, difficult to fabricate, dependent on critical materials, highly sensitive to contamination, impossible to characterize consistently, or incompatible with industrial manufacturing. The book therefore follows a broader progression: Function → Measurement → Manufacturing → Reliability → Lifecycle. This progression is applied across a wide range of nanomaterial systems. The research examines graphene, carbon nanotubes, nanodiamond, quantum-confined materials, transition-metal dichalcogenides, hexagonal boron nitride, van der Waals heterostructures, nanoporous solids, aerogels, metal-organic frameworks, covalent organic frameworks, nanocomposites, high-entropy nanostructures, metamaterials, metasurfaces, hierarchical materials, surface coatings, atomic-layer structures, self-assembled systems, DNA-based nanostructures, and emerging forms of programmable matter. A major theme of the book is surface physics. At small dimensions, a large fraction of atoms may exist near a surface or interface. Surface energy, adsorption, ligand chemistry, oxidation, contamination, catalytic activity, wetting, adhesion, and reconstruction can therefore become first-order engineering variables. The surface is no longer merely the boundary of a material. It may become one of the primary locations where function is created. Interfaces are treated with equal importance. Electronic transport, thermal resistance, mechanical transfer, optical coupling, ion motion, catalytic selectivity, and phase stability may all depend strongly on how two materials meet. This makes interface engineering central to the design of nanoscale systems. The book examines band alignment, interfacial strain, thermal boundary conductance, adhesion, charge transfer, defect segregation, interphase formation, and chemically engineered interfaces. Defects are also reconsidered. In conventional engineering, defects are often treated only as failures to be eliminated. At the nanoscale, defects may also create useful electronic states, catalytic sites, diffusion pathways, magnetic behavior, optical signatures, or mechanical responses. The challenge is therefore not simply defect elimination. It is defect control. This leads to a broader principle: Defect Engineering = Location + Density + Type + Stability + Function. The book explores vacancies, substitutions, dislocations, grain boundaries, stacking faults, edge states, pores, impurities, and radiation-induced defects as both risks and design variables. Two-dimensional materials form another major research domain. Graphene, transition-metal dichalcogenides, hBN, layered semiconductors, and van der Waals heterostructures create new opportunities for electronics, sensing, photonics, thermal management, membranes, catalysis, and quantum devices. However, the book repeatedly distinguishes intrinsic material properties from usable device performance. Crystal quality, substrate interactions, contact resistance, contamination, transfer damage, strain, encapsulation, and manufacturing yield may matter as much as the ideal properties of the material itself. Carbon nanostructures are examined through a similarly engineering-centered framework. Carbon nanotubes, graphene architectures, nanodiamond, carbon networks, and hybrid structures can offer unusual combinations of strength, conductivity, thermal transport, chemical stability, and low mass. But practical deployment depends on dispersion, alignment, interface quality, purity, contact formation, reproducibility, and scale-up. The book also explores metamaterials and metasurfaces. Here, function emerges not primarily from chemical composition but from engineered geometry. Electromagnetic, acoustic, mechanical, optical, and thermal behavior may be designed through subwavelength structure. This represents a major shift in materials engineering: Structure itself becomes part of the material definition. Nanocomposites extend the same principle into multiscale engineering. Nanoparticles, fibers, sheets, pores, interfaces, and hierarchical architectures can alter strength, toughness, conductivity, barrier performance, thermal behavior, sensing, and multifunctionality. But these systems introduce new problems in dispersion, percolation, agglomeration, interface stability, processing, and reproducibility. The book therefore treats hierarchical structure as both opportunity and complexity. Self-assembly and programmable matter represent one of the most forward-looking sections. Instead of manufacturing every feature directly, future materials may increasingly be designed through rules that cause components to organize themselves. DNA origami, molecular recognition, colloidal assembly, supramolecular systems, block copolymers, responsive particles, and reconfigurable structures suggest a future in which materials can be programmed through interaction rules. This creates a new engineering progression: Building Material → Structured Material → Responsive Material → Reconfigurable Material → Programmable Matter. Nanometrology is treated as a foundational part of the entire field. At the nanoscale, measurement is not simply an observation step added after fabrication. Measurement determines whether a claimed nanoscale effect is real, reproducible, comparable, and transferable across laboratories. Particle-size distributions, surface chemistry, roughness, thickness, crystallinity, defects, interfaces, local composition, mechanical properties, electronic states, and contamination all require appropriate measurement methods and uncertainty analysis. The book therefore treats metrology, reference materials, calibration, statistical interpretation, and interlaboratory reproducibility as part of nanomaterial engineering itself. Manufacturing is equally central. A remarkable nanostructure is not yet a technology. The research examines atomic layer deposition, chemical vapor deposition, nanoscale coatings, templating, directed self-assembly, nanoparticle synthesis, roll-to-roll processing, scalable composite fabrication, quality control, process windows, and closed-loop manufacturing. This leads to one of the book’s central industrial questions: Can the desired nanoscale structure still be produced when manufacturing moves from one sample to millions of components? Artificial intelligence and inverse design are also explored as emerging tools. AI may assist with materials discovery, surrogate modeling, structure-property prediction, synthesis planning, process optimization, uncertainty analysis, and autonomous experimentation. Closed-loop laboratories could connect: Hypothesis → Synthesis → Characterization → Model Update → New Experiment. However, the book emphasizes that AI cannot replace reliable measurement, physical understanding, or experimental validation. The final technological layer is lifecycle and responsible development. Nanomaterials may introduce new questions involving exposure, persistence, environmental release, recyclability, critical-material dependence, end-of-life recovery, occupational safety, and long-term ecological behavior. The book therefore integrates safer-by-design thinking directly into materials development rather than treating safety as an afterthought. title: Rethinking Metal-Mediated Electrochemical Ammonia Synthesis through Full-Cell Thermodynamics
abstract: Abstract Dissociative, metal-mediated electrochemical nitrogen reduction can achieve high selectivity under mild conditions, but its energy cost is often obscured by cathode-only accounting. Here, we develop a full-cell thermodynamic framework for metal-mediated ammonia electrosynthesis by decomposing the cycle into mediator generation, nitrogen incorporation, and protonation. We show that, once nitrogen incorporation and protonation are made downhill, the dominant lower bound on reversible electrical work is set by the mediator equilibrium potential. For Li-mediated nitrogen reduction, cathode-only Li generation already imposes a floor of approximately 9.12 eV per NH3, while full-cell accounting with anodic water oxidation raises the system-level cost further. Highly reducing mediators such as Li, Ca, and Mg preserve dissociative nitride chemistry but exceed practical energy benchmarks. The resulting design map identifies lower-energy routes through electrolyte-driven potential shifts, alloy or intercalation buffering, electrochemical nitridation, and non-nitride intermediates.
